Threat.value: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

vignette:
Dorothea Vance is a 78-year-old European American woman who has worked as a public defender for nearly four decades, a career built on the conviction that every person deserves a vigorous advocate regardless of what they are accused of. She is married, sharp-minded, and, until recently, the kind of woman who walked into a courtroom or a jail interview room without a second thought about her own safety. She is seeking help now, several months after an assault that she describes with a careful precision that suggests she has rehearsed the telling many times without ever quite making peace with it.

The incident occurred on a weekday evening in the parking structure adjacent to the courthouse where Dorothea has practiced for most of her professional life. She had stayed late reviewing case files and was walking alone to her car on the third level when a man approached her from behind, grabbed her by the shoulder, shoved her against a concrete pillar, and demanded her bag. The physical contact was brief but violent; she struck her head against the pillar and fell. He took her bag and ran. What stayed with her - what she returns to again and again in sessions - is not the moment of impact but the moment just before it: the sound of footsteps she had registered and then consciously dismissed, telling herself she was being foolish. She had heard him coming and done nothing. She has come to believe, with a certainty that feels to her like simple fact, that the world contains threats she is not equipped to detect in time, and that her own judgment about safety is fundamentally unreliable.

In the weeks that followed, Dorothea found herself reorganizing her behavior in ways that at first seemed reasonable and then became consuming. She began checking behind her whenever she walked anywhere - in the courthouse corridor, in the grocery store, in the parking lot of her church. The checking is not casual; she turns her head deliberately, accounting for each person in her wake, and if someone she has noted is still there when she checks again, something cold moves through her chest. She watches people in waiting rooms and hallways with an attention she once reserved for witnesses on the stand, reading posture and proximity and the direction of a gaze for signs of intent. She is certain, on some level she cannot fully articulate, that the information is there to be read if she looks carefully enough - that she simply failed to read it that evening in the parking structure.

Her work as a public defender has not stopped, but it has changed in texture. She meets clients in jail interview rooms, many of them young men charged with violent offenses, and she has always prided herself on her ability to be fully present with them, to listen without flinching. Now she finds herself tracking their movements across the small table with a vigilance that sits uneasily alongside her professional role. She has not spoken of this to colleagues. She is also easily startled in ways that embarrass her - a door slamming in the public defenders' office, a clerk appearing suddenly at her shoulder, the scrape of a chair in a conference room - and she has reacted visibly enough on several occasions that junior colleagues have noticed and asked if she is all right. She has told them she is tired.

Her husband has noticed the changes at home - the way she checks the locks, the way she positions herself in restaurants with her back to the wall - and has gently encouraged her to speak to someone. What finally moved her to make an appointment was a morning when she froze completely in the parking structure of the courthouse, unable to make herself walk to her car alone, and had to ask a security guard to accompany her. Standing there waiting for him, she felt a grief she could not name. What she is most afraid of, she said in her first session, is that she will never again be the person who walked into that building without fear. What she is most hoping for is something more modest: to stop feeling like a target.
